title: Events, the interval and proper time
summary: Conventions (SI, c explicit, signature (−,+,+,+) and the dictionary to Taylor–Wheeler and Tong); events and inertial frames; the invariant spacetime interval checked on the book's spark data; proper time of a uniformly moving clock derived from invariance; timelike, lightlike and spacelike separations; time measured in metres.

objectives.description: State the invariant interval in the (−,+,+,+) convention, translate it into the conventions of Taylor–Wheeler and Tong, and compute it from coordinate separations with units carried.
Derive τ = Δt√(1 − v²/c²) for a uniformly moving clock from the invariance of the interval, and check the limits v ≪ c and v → c.
Classify a pair of events as timelike, lightlike or spacelike and identify the frame (if any) in which they are co-located or simultaneous.
Explain the difference between coordinate time and proper time and why 'moving clocks run slow' is frame-dependent shorthand for a frame-independent statement.

preparation.description: Read Section 1.1 Parable of the Surveyors (printed pp. 1–4): rotation-invariant distance as the model for the interval.

Read Section 1.2 Surveying Spacetime (pp. 5–8): time in metres, c as a conversion factor, the two sparks, Tables 1-3 and 1-4, Eqs. (1-4)–(1-6). Note the book's sign convention and translate Eq. (1-6) into ours.
Work Sample Problem 1-1 Sparking at a Faster Rate (pp. 8–9) yourself before reading its solution.
Read Section 1.3 Events and Intervals Alone! (pp. 9–11): events as the primitive objects; wristwatch (proper) time.
Read Section 1.4 (pp. 11–13), especially the timelike/spacelike discussion and the 1983 definition of the metre, and Section 1.5 Unity of Spacetime (pp. 15–18).
Second account for a mathematician: Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, Section 7.3.1 The Invariant Interval (reference-only; uses the opposite sign convention, Δs² = c²Δt² − Δx²).

exitCheck.description: Use all three problems to review the objectives. The recorded checkpoint is the application/derivation below; acceptance of one exercise alone is not certification of every course outcome.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A negative squared interval means a mistake has been made.
commonMisconceptions.correction: In Lorentz geometry Δs² can be negative (timelike), zero (lightlike) or positive (spacelike); the sign is information, not an error. The book's Section 1.4 handclap example is a spacelike pair.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Moving clocks run slow, so the rocket clock is 'wrong' or 'slowed down'.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The rocket clock reads the proper time between two events it is present at; laboratory clocks read a coordinate time between the same events at different places. Both are correct measurements of different quantities; τ ≤ Δt follows from invariance of the interval.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Proper time is 'the time in the rest frame of the observer'.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Proper time belongs to a pair of events (or a worldline between them), not to an observer's frame: it is the time read by a clock present at both events. Different pairs of events have different proper clocks.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Two events with zero interval are the same event.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Zero interval means the events can be joined by a light flash (lightlike separation); they can be far apart in space and time. This is a genuine difference from Euclidean distance.
